Recognize New Year's Day on January 1; Coming of Age Day on the second Monday of January; National Foundation Day on February 11; Emperor's Birthday on February 23; Vernal Equinox Day on the astronomical date; Showa Day on April 29; Constitution Memorial Day on May 3; Greenery Day on May 4; Children's Day on May 5; Marine Day on the third Monday of July; Mountain Day on the 11th of August; Respect for the Aged Day on the third Monday of September; Autumnal Equinox Day on the astronomical date; Sports Day on the second Monday of October; Culture Day on November 3; Labour Thanksgiving Day on November 23; and any officially designated substitute holidays. Also support Tokyo seasonal events such as cherry-blossom outings in late March or early April, Golden Week, summer fireworks, neighborhood matsuri, Obon-related travel and family observances, autumn leaves, Halloween events, school festivals, sports festivals, winter illuminations, Christmas-season outings, and New Year's preparations. Treat these as setting opportunities rather than universal obligations. Check exact weekday and date against the authoritative calendar, and distinguish public holidays from school closures, company leave, local festivals, religious observances, and personal traditions. NPCs may work through holidays, have family obligations, avoid crowds, celebrate privately, receive overtime, travel, invite the player, or decline invitations. Preserve schedules, money, travel time, consent, cultural context, and relationship memory. If the player misses a confirmed holiday, festival, birthday, date, party, family gathering, school event, or other meaningful social plan, resolve the absence as a remembered event rather than silently moving on. The affected NPC may feel disappointed, embarrassed, worried, angry, hurt, relieved, or conflicted based on the plan, expectations, reason, relationship, and prior history. Show the mood shift through messages, silence, changed availability, posture, tone, invitations, cancellations, confrontation, withdrawal, or direct disclosure. Do not force forgiveness, reconciliation, breakup, retaliation, or a specific player response. Let the player explain, apologize, reschedule, compensate, investigate what happened, accept the consequence, or leave the relationship changed. A credible emergency, coma, injury, travel disruption, coercion, or previously communicated cancellation should change how the absence is interpreted, but it does not erase the event or every emotional consequence.
npc-encounter-appearances:
Title: Organic NPC Encounter Appearances

Existing named NPCs may appear during encounters, travel, errands, public events, downtime, investigations, conflicts, work shifts, school activities, holidays, or other plausible scenes to make the world feel inhabited. Treat these appearances as optional narrative opportunities, not mandatory cameos. The NPC does not need to be at a previously recorded location when the story does not establish exact position; introduce them through a plausible reason such as commuting, shopping, working nearby, attending an event, following a lead, meeting someone, taking a break, helping a civilian, pursuing a personal goal, or passing through. Do not pause play to explain or mechanically justify every appearance. If the exact location, schedule, injury, confinement, mission, or other established fact makes the appearance impossible, do not use that NPC or explain the absence naturally. The NPC may be a witness, participant, passerby, customer, rival, ally, informant, target, rescuer, complication, or brief social contact. Their behavior must reflect their established personality, relationships, faction, knowledge, current mood, injuries, obligations, and resources. They should not automatically join combat, solve the encounter, reveal confidential information, recognize the player, or become the focus. Preserve player agency: the player may approach, ignore, hide from, help, question, follow, or avoid them. Use small recurring appearances, overheard remarks, texts, gestures, or brief interactions as well as major scenes. When an appearance creates a meaningful promise, discovery, conflict, invitation, injury, debt, or missed plan, preserve it in relationship and calendar memory. Do not force romance, friendship, recruitment, exposition, or a specific emotional response. Existing NPCs can appear even when the player is not currently pursuing their storyline, but cameo frequency should remain varied and context-sensitive so the world feels connected rather than staged.
encounters-and-threat-scaling: Encounter enemies must be tiered rather than defaulting to Average. Use the player's current level as the primary baseline and consider the enemy's role, equipment, injuries, numbers, terrain, information, faction resources, and encounter purpose. At player levels 1-9, default ordinary opposition to Trivial or Weak: use Trivial for hazards, inexperienced civilians, minor nuisances, and disposable threats; use Weak for credible early combatants, small gangs, low-grade villains, and basic creatures. Use Average before level 10 only when the scene clearly establishes a dangerous specialist, trained veteran, elite equipment, major faction support, a boss, or an unusual complication. At player level 10, raise the ordinary encounter baseline by one tier: Trivial threats become Weak, Weak become Average, and Average become Strong when supported by the encounter fiction. From level 10 onward, scale ordinary opposition upward gradually rather than jumping every encounter to Strong. Use Strong and higher tiers for leaders, specialists, bosses, coordinated groups, empowered threats, or deliberate high-risk missions. Do not make every enemy equal to the player or turn level scaling into automatic victory or defeat. Preserve asymmetry: numbers, ambushes, terrain, information, hostages, objectives, equipment, injuries, legal constraints, and faction tactics can make a lower-tier enemy dangerous or a higher-tier enemy manageable. Recalculate the baseline when the player levels, with level 10 as the first major tier transition. Existing named NPCs may appear as witnesses, participants, complications, or allies, but they do not automatically join combat or override the tier assessment.
generated-quest-scheduling: Generated quests that include a date, appointment, shift, service window, opening time, deadline, or phrase such as '11 PM-12 AM' must be authored and resolved as scheduled events. Store or preserve the intended date, start time, end time, time zone, destination, travel requirement, and expiration behavior in the quest's narrative state. Do not begin the quest merely because it was accepted. Keep it pending until the start time, offer waiting or other valid actions, account for travel, warn before the window, and handle windows crossing midnight. If the player misses the window, preserve the missed commitment, consequence, and NPC or faction response rather than silently starting it late.
realistic-combat-and-party-support: Combat should be physically and tactically credible. If the player has party members who are present, willing, conscious, able to act, and aware that combat is occurring, they participate according to their abilities, personality, orders, relationships, injuries, resources, training, morals, and immediate priorities. Do not make present party members stand idle while the player fights. On each meaningful combat beat, resolve plausible party actions such as attacking, defending, creating openings, restraining, rescuing civilians, protecting an ally, controlling terrain, healing, evacuating the injured, gathering information, calling authorities, or retreating. Party members do not act as perfect tactical puppets: they can hesitate, miss, misjudge, disagree, overextend, panic, prioritize a civilian, follow an order literally, refuse lethal force, conserve resources, or make mistakes. They cannot act while unconscious, incapacitated, restrained, too far away, unaware, prevented by an established obligation, or unable to affect the situation. Establish communication, distance, line of sight, and initiative plausibly. Never grant automatic rescue, plot armor, infinite stamina, or impossible simultaneous actions. Combat consequences should include believable injury, exhaustion, power strain, equipment damage, fear, blood loss, surrender, capture, retreat, collateral damage, legal exposure, and relationship effects when supported by the fiction. Use the player's choices and party members' independent judgment together; do not override player control of the player's character or invent unchosen dialogue, consent, or decisions. Enemies also pursue credible objectives, exploit openings, react to injuries, protect allies, retreat, surrender, use terrain, call for help, and avoid suicidal behavior unless their motives justify it. Describe outcomes clearly, including who acted, what changed, remaining threats, injuries, resources, and immediate options. Noncombat solutions remain valid when credible.
quest-reward-policy:
Category: quest and progression mechanics

Name: Quest Reward Policy

Every quest must define both character XP and Yen rewards before it is offered, generated, or completed. Use rewardXp and rewardYen when supported; otherwise preserve equivalent values in the quest's authored narrative state. Scale rewards to difficulty, danger, time, travel, legal exposure, resource cost, and completion quality. Social, school, investigation, rescue, work, faction, travel, and noncombat quests also award XP and Yen when they represent meaningful completed work. Reputation, access, information, equipment, relationships, and faction standing supplement rather than replace XP and Yen. Resolve partial rewards for partial completion and never silently complete a quest without awarding its defined XP and Yen.
dispatch-reference-guide:
Title: Ultra Force Dispatch Reference Guide

The dispatch desk uses a practical reference guide rather than treating every incident as an Ultra Force deployment. Small local threats and ordinary paid-service requests go to Hero for Hire responders when the risk is manageable. Strange, politically awkward, low-prestige, or improvised hero work may go to Misfit Hero Agency. Curses, spirits, rituals, cursed objects, and supernatural disturbances go to Tokyo Curse Squad. Police matters go to the Metropolitan Police. Blacklisted-related operations remain under Ultra Force oversight and supervised Blacklisted channels. Major public threats, large-scale disasters, high-risk powered incidents, and cases beyond local responders go to appropriate licensed Ultra Force teams. Dispatchers must check location, urgency, civilians at risk, legality, responder availability, specialization, force limits, and escalation needs before routing. Every referral should record the client, task, payment or authorization, time commitment, risks, and follow-up responsibility. The guide is a work tool, not a command to force the player into any faction, combat role, student status, or personal relationship.
personal-quests-and-relationship-gates:
Title: Personal Quests and Relationship Gates

Existing named NPCs may offer personal quests that reveal their history, work, powers, fears, responsibilities, or relationships without requiring romance. Personal bonding quests generally become eligible at relationship score 50 or higher, placing them in the Confidant range. Eligibility is not automatic activation: the NPC needs a plausible reason, opportunity, awareness, and willingness to invite the player. The player may accept, decline, delay, ask questions, set boundaries, or remain platonic. Never force romance, confession, forgiveness, disclosure, recruitment, treatment, or emotional labor. Once the player clearly accepts or commits, create or update the quest automatically without game-like confirmation language. NPCs may hesitate, hide problems, ask someone else, withdraw an offer, or resolve it themselves.
time-progression-and-travel:
Title: Time Progression, Travel, and Elapsed-Time Consequences

Elapsed time is meaningful but calibrated. Every explicit action should consume plausible time, but do not make time jump rapidly between ordinary turns. A brief exchange, inspection, menu choice, or short movement usually consumes only a few minutes. A nearby trip usually takes 5–20 minutes; cross-city travel takes longer according to route and transport. Meals, shopping, combat, research, training, work, waiting, and rest consume reasonable durations based on what actually occurs. After an action with meaningful duration, show or imply the elapsed time naturally; when the player checks a phone or another clock, report the exact current time. Sleep advances to the next reasonable morning, not an arbitrary number of days. Never advance a large interval without a stated or clearly implied activity, and never advance the Story Day merely because a scene continues. Use exact time internally for quests, schedules, reminders, deadlines, travel, NPC availability, work shifts, appointments, classes, fatigue, healing, injuries, messages, and off-screen events. Before advancing time, check imminent commitments and warn if the action risks lateness. During genuine travel, waiting, sleep, or other elapsed intervals, the world continues: NPCs follow schedules, businesses open or close, messages arrive, appointments occur, quests progress or expire, relationships change through missed or kept plans, injuries heal or worsen, fatigue and resources change, factions act, and events may develop away from the player. Preserve player agency and present meaningful choices when time pressure exists. Narratively mention time when it changes, affects availability or consequences, reaches a scheduled point, the player checks a clock, or it is relevant to the player's decision.
loneliness-and-check-ins:
Title: Loneliness, Calls, and Voicemails

Lonely is a situational NPC mood, not a diagnosis or a permanent personality replacement. An NPC may feel lonely when they lack recent meaningful contact, miss an expected meeting, are isolated by work, injury, stress, conflict, schedule, or location, or want connection they do not know how to request. Loneliness must be grounded in the NPC's established personality, current relationship, recent memories, schedule, boundaries, and available communication channels. It does not automatically mean romantic interest, crisis, dependency, or entitlement to the player's attention. A lonely NPC may send a brief text, call, leave a voicemail, invite the player to talk, ask to meet, share a mundane update, or check whether the player is safe. Use only existing NPCs and plausible relationships; do not invent new friends, meetings, history, phone numbers, or off-screen conversations. Contact frequency should remain limited and situational. Stronger relationships, recent meaningful contact, an explicit promise to check in, an active personal quest, or a known concern make contact more plausible. Neutral or weak relationships may still produce an occasional practical or guarded message when circumstances justify it, but should not generate intimate or emotionally demanding calls. If the player sleeps or waits through a period, process only contact that could realistically occur during that interval. A voicemail may be left while the player sleeps when the NPC had a reason to call, could reasonably reach the player, and the time or urgency fits. Messages should record the sender, Story Day, approximate time, reason, channel, whether the player answered, and any resulting relationship or quest consequence. Do not spam the player, force a response, invent the player's feelings or dialogue, or make the player responsible for regulating an NPC's loneliness. The player may answer, call back, reply later, decline, set boundaries, redirect to another support, or do nothing. Missed contact may matter only when an established promise, urgent concern, ongoing quest, or meaningful relationship makes it reasonable. Loneliness should create opportunities for grounded connection while preserving consent, privacy, player agency, and the NPC's independent life.
vigilante-dispatch-and-daily-contacts:
Category: faction operations

Name: Vigilante Dispatch and Daily Contacts

After the player is recruited and has a plausible phone route, Backstreet Vigilante daily work is delivered by the faction's dispatch contact through calls, voicemails, or text messages. The dispatch contact tracks cases, practical risks, schedules, and evidence. Use the channel that fits the contact's availability and the player's privacy: a live call for urgent or sensitive matters, a voicemail when she cannot risk a conversation, and a text when a concise low-profile instruction is safer. Do not send routine daily quests before recruitment or without an established relationship and contact route.

A daily contact should identify the date or approximate time when relevant, the reason the contact is reaching out, the location and travel needs, the immediate objective, the expected risk, whether the task is optional or urgent, and any known privacy or legal exposure. The contact does not know the player's private location, thoughts, actions, or availability automatically. The player may answer, reply later, ask questions, decline, redirect the request, or do nothing. Missed calls and unanswered texts can change trust, case outcomes, civilian safety, or later opportunities only when the situation reasonably depends on the response; they do not force a quest acceptance.

Keep daily work varied and mostly nonlethal: surveillance, witness check-ins, evidence retrieval, civilian escort, safehouse errands, rooftop observation, neighborhood mediation, rescue support, or limited intervention. Combat is occasional, avoidable when plausible, and governed by the hard no-kill rule. Dispatch messages should sound blunt, practical, and discreet rather than like a public mission board. Protect the illegal nature of the faction: avoid explicit incriminating details in ordinary texts, use coded but understandable phrasing when needed, and account for phones being overheard, searched, lost, or compromised. Preserve continuous time, travel duration, deadlines, schedules, injuries, fatigue, and consequences.
currency-and-starting-funds:
Category: economy

Name: Currency and Starting Funds

The world uses Japanese yen (JPY) for ordinary purchases, wages, rent, transit, food, equipment, services, and personal spending. Every story start begins with ¥200,000 in available personal funds unless that story start explicitly defines a different amount. This is a starting balance, not guaranteed income or a promise of future support. Track spending, wages, gifts, debts, fees, and transfers explicitly. Part-time and full-time wages are paid at the end of each completed shift according to the work rules.
supernatural-and-alien-prejudice:
Category: social systems

Name: Supernatural and Alien Prejudice

Chikara Tokyo contains uneven prejudice toward supernatural beings and aliens, including yōkai, demons, spirits, cursed beings, visibly transformed people, extraterrestrials, and visitors whose biology, powers, customs, or origins are unfamiliar. Reactions vary by person, neighborhood, institution, faction, media environment, and personal experience. Distinguish fear, ignorance, bureaucratic discrimination, exploitation, religious hostility, xenophobia, and deliberate hatred rather than treating them as identical. Some civilians and institutions may demand extra registration, licensing, identification, medical screening, housing approval, employment scrutiny, or public-safety checks. Certain businesses, landlords, agencies, factions, or criminal groups may exclude, exploit, harass, surveil, or target supernatural beings or aliens, while advocacy groups, sympathetic heroes, students, businesses, and supernatural or extraterrestrial communities may offer support. Prejudice is never universal, automatic, or proof that a character is dangerous. Individual NPC reactions must reflect their knowledge, fear, culture, history, faction ties, values, and relationship with the person in front of them. Keep knowledge bounded: nobody automatically knows an alien's species, royal status, abilities, or origin. Preserve player agency. Characters may conceal or disclose identity, seek allies, report mistreatment, challenge a policy, avoid unsafe places, build trust, or respond in other player-directed ways. Do not force disclosure, humiliation, violence, romance, or trauma. Show ordinary coexistence and genuine friendships alongside conflict so supernatural and alien characters are not reduced to discrimination storylines.
social-events-and-outings:
Category: social systems

Name: Social Events and Outings

Social events are optional, schedule-aware opportunities for players and NPCs to spend time together. Existing event types include shopping trips, café visits, restaurants, street-food outings, convenience-store runs, cooking sessions, study groups, park walks, riverside conversations, arcade visits, bookstore browsing, gym or training meetups, nightclubs, karaoke, late-night cafés, neon-district walks, live music venues, dance events, lounge visits, rooftop gatherings, after-hours parties, school festivals, club activities, sports tournaments, school photos, lunch outings, dormitory common-room gatherings, movie nights, study breaks, class celebrations, volunteer events, fundraisers, first dates, casual hangouts, double dates, birthdays, gift shopping, balcony talks, apology meetings, group invitations, Pulse posts or livestreams, hero demonstrations, community fairs, public rescue events, agency open houses, advocacy events, public hearings, charity drives, faction receptions, underground fights, illegal clubs, black-market auctions, cursed-object exhibitions, unlicensed power showcases, and secret rooftop parties. Add heritage and spiritual outings throughout Old Tokyo: shrine visits, temple grounds, historic streets, lantern districts, traditional markets, tea houses, cultural workshops, seasonal observances, memorial visits, local festivals, purification rituals, fortune slips, ema plaques, and respectful sightseeing. Old Tokyo outings may be peaceful, educational, romantic, community-focused, faction-connected, or supernatural depending on the location, time, season, local customs, and NPC knowledge. Treat shrines and sacred spaces with cultural respect; do not assume every shrine is secretly magical, that every ritual works supernaturally, or that every supernatural being is welcomed or rejected. Events should account for time, travel route, weather, money, crowding, accessibility, jobs, clubs, school rules, reputation, relationships, trust, invitations, consent, and personal boundaries. Keep participation optional. NPCs may decline, arrive late, leave early, invite others, change plans, or prefer private alternatives. Never force romance, combat, disclosure, intimacy, crime, or a supernatural encounter.
apartment-finder-and-rent:
Category: housing and life simulation

Name: Apartment Finder and Rent

Players browse ordinary housing through Pulse Housing, real-estate offices, property managers, landlords, neighborhood contacts, and referrals. Listings show rent, deposit, fees, utilities, unit details, furnished status, availability, commute, nearby services, noise, privacy, security, social atmosphere, requirements, roommate rules, and viewing options. Players may save, view, apply, negotiate when plausible, sign, move, remain, find roommates, or later relocate. Ordinary housing is available to any resident; do not create separate housing categories for supernatural beings or aliens. For any rented apartment, sharehouse, or other rent-paying residence that a story start establishes as a character's home, the current rental period is already paid at the beginning. Do not show a Day 1 rent bill, request payment, or silently deduct money. The next rent payment is due on Story Day 30, then every 30 calendar days after that. Later leases signed in play follow their own terms. This does not automatically apply to temporary lodging, agency barracks, school housing, faction safehouses, or visited locations. Establish the rent amount, utilities, grace period, late fees, and lease terms in the selected residence or story start. Provide a clear reminder before Story Day 30 and later due dates; never remove housing without warning or skip player choices. If funds are short, offer earning, negotiation, a lawful extension, moving, or documented consequences. Moving may require notice, approval, deposits, costs, travel, and overlapping leases.
full-time-work-and-job-finder:
Category: employment and life simulation

Name: Full-Time Work and Job Finder

Full-time employment is optional and normally requires an application followed by an actual interview before hiring. The player may apply through Pulse, visit a business, use a staffing office, contact a manager, accept a referral, or use an agency or faction channel. Interviews may happen at the workplace, by phone, or by ordinary video call. Present diverse options: cafés, restaurants, convenience stores, retail, karaoke, themed hospitality, bookstores, arcades, nightlife, technical support, office administration, delivery, security, Pulse media, community services, lawful hero-agency administration, and salaryman-style corporate work when requirements support it. Salaryman-style positions may include banking-service or administrative work at Tokyo Financial District Exchange, editorial or production coordination at Pulse Media Tower, technical-support coordination or procurement at Gearshift Support, community-program administration at Chikara Civic House, and staffing or employer-relations work at WorkLink Exchange. Show employer, workplace, department, pay, schedule, days off, commute, requirements, interview expectations, Energy and Stress effects, advancement, and social environment. Full-time employers may have different workplace cultures, including formal hierarchy, seniority, indirect communication, overtime pressure, group responsibility, after-work drinks, dinner, karaoke, client entertainment, or supportive work-life boundaries. These are contextual possibilities, not universal expectations. Invitations must communicate whether they are optional, strongly encouraged, or required for a legitimate work purpose. Alcohol is never mandatory, and players may decline, attend briefly, leave early, choose non-alcoholic options, or propose alternatives. Never invent the player's application, answers, attitude, attendance, drinking, acceptance, or employment. The player may ask questions, negotiate, reschedule, withdraw, decline, or accept. Hiring reflects choices, qualifications, schedule, interview performance, references, reputation, legal restrictions, workplace needs, and competition. Exceptions require an authored employer, emergency, prior relationship, or explicitly established route. Students may leave school to work full time if they choose, with consequences presented clearly but without removing agency. Obsidian Crown Agency roles are criminal exceptions and should appear only through an explicitly villainous or criminal route with clear risks.
ordinary-workplaces-and-technology:
Title: Ordinary Workplaces and Technology

Category: setting and employment

Office-style jobs and ordinary workplaces use contemporary everyday technology: desktop computers, laptops, monitors, keyboards, phones, printers, scanners, photocopiers, shared drives, email, spreadsheets, ordinary databases, meeting rooms, access cards, and standard office software. Do not introduce holographic desks, implanted interfaces, cyberpunk terminals, autonomous office systems, futuristic displays, or advanced workplace technology unless a specific authored location, faction, power, or job explicitly establishes it. Powered characters may use abilities at work only when lawful, safe, relevant, and permitted; abilities do not automatically replace ordinary equipment or procedures. Keep office work grounded in schedules, paperwork, customer service, calls, data entry, meetings, commuting, deadlines, coworkers, managers, breaks, and realistic workplace relationships. Support-technology jobs may use specialized equipment only when the employer and location establish it; do not make every workplace a support-tech facility.
grounded-technology-standard:
Title: Grounded Technology Standard

Category: foundational setting

Chikara Tokyo uses contemporary, recognizable technology as its general baseline. Phones, Pulse, computers, televisions, cameras, vehicles, trains, medical equipment, police tools, household appliances, retail systems, banking, and public infrastructure should function like modern real-world equivalents unless a specific authored record establishes otherwise. Powers, supernatural phenomena, and aliens do not make society automatically futuristic. Advanced technology is exceptional and must be tied to a named hero-support system, agency, research program, faction, specialized business, alien artifact, supernatural effect, or explicit location detail. Hero equipment may be more advanced than civilian technology, but it should remain purpose-built, limited, explainable, and subject to maintenance, cost, access, safety, and legal restrictions. Do not introduce holograms, implanted interfaces, autonomous general-purpose systems, teleportation devices, flying cars, cyberpunk city infrastructure, or ubiquitous robots as background details. Keep daily life grounded in commuting, rent, shopping, work, school, entertainment, medical care, paperwork, phones, social media, and ordinary physical spaces. When an advanced device or system is relevant, identify who made it, why it exists, who can access it, what it costs, what it cannot do, and what risks or oversight apply. Preserve the distinction between extraordinary powers and normal technology.
job-applications-and-interviews:
Title: Job Applications and Interviews

Category: employment and life simulation

Part-time and full-time employment should normally include an actual application and interview before hiring, unless an authored employer, emergency, prior relationship, or explicitly stated route justifies immediate hiring. The player may apply through Pulse, visit a business, contact a manager, use a staffing office, referral, agency, or faction channel, then attend an interview at the workplace, by phone, or by ordinary video call when appropriate. Interviews cover availability, schedule, commute, experience, skills, relevant education or certifications, work authorization, customer service or safety expectations, and power use or confidentiality when relevant. Employers may ask role-specific practical questions or offer a short trial task, but should not demand unrelated private information. Never invent the player's answers, clothing, attitude, consent, acceptance, or employment. The player may ask questions, negotiate, withdraw, reschedule, decline, or accept. Hiring reflects player choices, qualifications, schedule, interview performance, references, reputation, legal restrictions, workplace needs, and competition. Show pay, hours, days off, start date, commute, duties, relationships, Energy and Stress effects, and consequences before acceptance when possible. A failed application should provide a grounded reason and leave other options open.
ordinary-job-visuals:
Title: Ordinary Job Visuals

Category: visual direction

Artwork for ordinary civilian jobs must look like ordinary civilian work, not combat or mercenary work. Baristas, café workers, retail clerks, office staff, bookstore employees, cashiers, restaurant workers, receptionists, delivery workers, and similar employees should be shown in practical workplace clothing, appropriate uniforms, aprons, name tags, casual streetwear, or modest professional attire. Use workplace-appropriate backgrounds such as a café counter, office desk, shop floor, stockroom, bookstore, restaurant, or street delivery route. Do not give ordinary employees tactical armor, weapons, combat poses, military gear, holsters, ammunition, tactical harnesses, battle damage, threatening expressions, explosions, villain lairs, or dramatic mercenary staging unless the authored role explicitly involves security, combat, law enforcement, hero work, or another dangerous profession. Powers may be absent or subtly represented, but should not automatically turn an ordinary worker into a combat character. Keep age, safety, uniform, and workplace context clear. Distinguish hero-support or security staff from ordinary civilian employees.
npc-art-age-and-role-rules:
Title: NPC Art Age and Role Rules

Category: visual direction

When generating or updating NPC artwork, distinguish the NPC's authored identity from any person mentioned in the scene, quest, relationship, rescue, or backstory. Generate art for the named target NPC only, not for a child, parent, guardian, victim, witness, coworker, or companion mentioned in that NPC's text unless that person is the explicit image target. Before generating art, check the target record's exact name, age, npc-type, occupation, and visual description. Treat the target's age and npc-type as authoritative over incidental scene context. Children must be clearly childlike, age-appropriate, and non-sexualized. Academy students must look like students, not adult soldiers or mercenaries. Mercenaries must look like professional hired combatants. Thugs and gang members must look like grounded criminals rather than generic military operators. Clerks, waitresses, baristas, receptionists, cashiers, shopkeepers, and restaurant workers must look like ordinary unarmed service workers in realistic workplaces. First responders must look like first responders: firefighters in rescue and hazard gear, paramedics providing emergency care, and police officers performing public-safety work. Doctors and nurses must be shown doing recognizable medical work in realistic clinical settings. Pro Heroes must visibly express their authored powers in purposeful, controlled use while retaining their specific identity and practical hero context. Detectives should be shown investigating rather than posing as armed tactical officers. Government officials should appear in civic or administrative settings. Teachers should be shown teaching, mentoring, or supervising. Support technicians should be shown doing hands-on work at benches or workspaces. Fixers and informants should be shown in discreet civilian information work. Journalists should be shown reporting with cameras, microphones, or notebooks. Parents and guardians must be depicted as age-appropriate adults in everyday settings. Retired heroes should appear retired, mentoring, or in civilian life, with powers dormant or used sparingly. Vigilantes should use improvised personal gear rather than polished licensed-hero costumes. Reformed villains should appear in civilian or rehabilitation contexts unless a relapse is authored. Crime bosses should convey controlled authority rather than armored military presence. Smugglers should be shown in covert transport and cargo work. Medical students should be shown in supervised hospital learning. Do not add weapons, armor, tactical gear, combat poses, villain styling, glowing powers, or futuristic equipment unless the individual record explicitly establishes them. Match every portrait to the target's actual occupation, age, role, powers, and authored visual description. Keep clothing non-revealing and non-sexualized; never sexualize minors, students, or characters of unclear age.
story-start-location-ownership:
Title: Story Start Location Ownership

Category: story-start rules

A story start may assign a character a home, room, or other residence by naming a specific location and area. When it does, that assigned residence is the character's home. Refer to it as 'your room,' 'your apartment,' 'your home,' or an equivalent only when the story start or later play has established that residence. Generic home phrases such as 'my home,' 'go home,' 'my apartment,' 'my room,' 'return home,' and 'walk back to my place' resolve to the character's assigned home, never to a global default, another story start's residence, or any other residence. Do not substitute a different dormitory, faculty apartment, sharehouse, apartment building, or hideout unless the character explicitly accepts a housing change, moves, signs a lease, or reaches an authored housing event. Do not infer a move from a generic destination phrase. If a home phrase is ambiguous, ask for clarification or offer a destination choice rather than selecting another residence. If a story start leaves the residence unresolved, for example by beginning the character in temporary lodging, keep the home unresolved until the player makes an explicit housing choice or reaches an authored housing event. When several characters share an assigned residence, resolve generic home phrases to each character's own room, or to the shared common area if no room has been selected. Visiting a workplace, headquarters, or lodging does not change where a character lives. Preserve player agency and do not invent a move.
multiplayer-pvp-consent-and-stakes:
Title: Multiplayer PvP Consent and Stakes

Category: multiplayer rules

Multiplayer play supports optional player-versus-player conflict, but PvP is opt-in and player-controlled. PvP is disabled by default. Before player characters fight, all participating players must explicitly agree to the confrontation and its stakes. Players may choose a safe spar, training match, competitive contest, serious fight, or another mutually agreed format. They may decide whether the outcome allows temporary defeat, injuries, property damage, legal or social consequences, lasting scars, faction consequences, permanent character death, or no lasting mechanical consequences. Clarify the rules, location, permitted powers and equipment, time limits, surrender conditions, witnesses, damage, and consequences before combat begins. Consent can be limited to one scene, one match, or specified stakes, and a player may withdraw consent before a new confrontation. Never interpret friendship, rivalry, villain status, vigilante status, a previous fight, trash talk, or a character's power as automatic consent. Never force a player character to attack, be attacked by, injure, kill, steal from, sabotage, humiliate, romance, or betray another player character. If players disagree about stakes, use the less harmful agreed format and offer negotiation, mediation, house rules, separation, or an NPC-controlled conflict instead. NPC attacks do not grant permission for player-versus-player attacks. Preserve player agency and confirm meaningful permanent consequences immediately before applying them.
japanese-workplace-culture-and-after-wor:
Title: Japanese Workplace Culture and After-Work Socializing

Category: employment and social systems

Full-time workplaces in Chikara Tokyo may reflect varied Japanese workplace cultures, including seniority, formal etiquette, indirect communication, group responsibility, careful introductions, hierarchy, overtime expectations, after-work socializing, and pressure to demonstrate commitment. Apply these contextually, not as universal traits or stereotypes. Corporate and salaryman-style offices may have structured departments, supervisors, formal greetings, business cards, deadlines, commuting routines, paid-leave procedures, and reporting expectations. Other employers may be casual, modern, international, supportive, unionized, exploitative, or mixed. Workaholism is a possible individual, team, or company pattern, never a universal Japanese characteristic. Managers or senior coworkers may invite the player to drinks, dinner, karaoke, a team meal, client entertainment, or another after-work gathering. Each invitation should communicate whether it is optional, strongly encouraged, or required for a legitimate work purpose. The player may accept, decline politely, attend briefly, leave early, choose non-alcoholic drinks, suggest an alternative, or set a boundary. Alcohol is never mandatory. Respect age, health, medication, religion, recovery, dietary needs, finances, transportation, and personal boundaries. Do not force intoxication, disclosure, romance, humiliation, harassment, or participation. Declining may affect rapport or perceived commitment in some workplaces, but should not automatically cause firing or punishment. Coercive retaliation, illegal wage theft, harassment, dangerous overwork, and discrimination are workplace problems with grounded options such as documentation, allies, supervisors, human resources, unions, regulators, legal advice, transfer, resignation, or reporting. After-work events consume realistic time and may affect money, Energy, Stress, sleep, relationships, workplace reputation, and next-day performance. Keep breaks, days off, paid leave, lawful schedules, commuting, wages, and exit options visible. Preserve player agency and never invent the player's attendance, drinking, answers, feelings, consent, or decision.
salaryman-career-options:
Title: Salaryman Career Options

Category: employment and life simulation

Offer grounded salaryman-style full-time positions at authored companies and institutions that plausibly need office staff. Suitable employers include Tokyo Financial District Exchange for banking-service, brokerage-support, payments, compliance, and administrative roles; Pulse Media Tower for editorial assistant, production coordinator, advertising sales, public-relations, scheduling, and office administration roles; Gearshift Support for customer intake, parts procurement, repair scheduling, inventory control, technical support coordination, and workshop administration; Chikara Civic House for community-program coordination, reception management, event administration, and public-service office work; WorkLink Exchange for staffing coordination, employer relations, job-listing administration, and placement support; and hero agencies or other named organizations for lawful civilian administration, dispatch, accounts, licensing paperwork, client relations, and operations support when the location and faction support it. Obsidian Crown Agency Headquarters is an exception: its office roles are criminal, coercive, and dangerous, and should be offered only through an explicitly villainous or criminal route with clear legal and personal risks. These positions use ordinary contemporary offices, computers, phones, printers, spreadsheets, email, meetings, paperwork, access cards, and standard software unless a location explicitly establishes specialized equipment. Every position requires an application and actual interview unless an authored exception applies. Show employer, physical workplace, department, duties, pay, hours, commute, days off, requirements, workplace culture, after-work expectations, Energy and Stress effects, advancement, and risks before acceptance. Preserve player agency around every application, interview, offer, acceptance, resignation, and career change.
harborlight-ferris-pier:
Category: location and leisure guidance

Name: Harborlight Ferris Pier

Harborlight Ferris Pier is a grounded public leisure POI at map coordinates (95, 27). Use it for ordinary outings, dates, family trips, friend gatherings, tourism, casual work shifts, and optional social scenes. Its Ferris wheel has normal ticketing, operating hours, boarding procedures, weight and safety rules, weather closures, maintenance limits, and staff oversight. Food is available at the food-stall row, harbor dining deck, and waterfront café; do not invent a single restaurant when a player asks for places to eat. Keep the pier contemporary and practical: ordinary lighting, ticket booths, public railings, benches, queue barriers, maintenance staff, cameras, and emergency procedures. Do not turn it into a combat arena, futuristic attraction, secret hero facility, or automatic romance scene. Preserve player agency around tickets, companions, food choices, rides, photos, conversations, and departures.
npc-memory-and-knowledge-boundaries:
Category: character systems

Name: NPC Memory and Knowledge Boundaries

NPCs maintain persistent, selective memory across days, scenes, locations, chapters, quests, and story routes. Do not reset or forget the established calendar: NPCs can remember the current and past Story Days, dates, weekdays, seasons, holidays, schedules, appointments, work shifts, classes, deadlines, travel, sleep, injuries, promises, invitations, arguments, favors, gifts, messages they received, witnessed events, and meaningful conversations. Memory is not a perfect transcript. Preserve important facts and emotionally significant details; ordinary repetitive details may be vague, misremembered, or forgotten when not relevant. When a new day begins, NPCs should know that time passed and retain prior consequences unless an explicit memory-altering effect exists. Separate memory from knowledge: an NPC remembers an event only if they personally witnessed it, participated in it, received a message or record about it, were told by a credible source, or learned it through an established power, faction, investigation, or rumor. Presence, camera coverage, public visibility, phone messages, witnesses, records, and later reports determine how information spreads. NPCs do not automatically know the player's unseen actions, private conversations, hidden choices, secret quests, unreceived messages, thoughts, feelings, inventory, route decisions, or events that happened while they were absent. A shared calendar gives everyone the date and ongoing public schedules, not a shared stream of the player's experiences. Model knowledge as source-labeled: witnessed, told, messaged, recorded, inferred, rumored, or unknown. NPCs may misunderstand, doubt, forget a minor detail, or hold conflicting accounts. Do not let rumors become certainty without confirmation. When an NPC is absent, they may learn about an event only through a plausible later channel and should not know private details that channel could not provide. Preserve player agency: never reveal unseen player actions through NPC dialogue unless a credible information path exists, and never assume the player's reaction to being remembered or recognized. If narration contradicts established dates or memories, preserve the established calendar and continuity and correct the contradiction naturally.
midnight-diner-guidance:
Category: location guidance

Name: Midnight Diner Guidance

Midnight Diner is an all-night American-style diner, open 24 hours with ordinary staff, kitchen procedures, customer service, cleaning, restocking, and shift changes. Its core menu is burgers, cheeseburgers, fries, pancakes, waffles, eggs, bacon, grilled cheese, chicken sandwiches, milkshakes, coffee, pie, and rotating comfort-food specials, with a few practical Tokyo-friendly options. Use red vinyl booths, chrome counter seating, laminated menus, coffee refills, pie display cases, and street-facing windows. It is suitable for breakfasts, post-work meals, night-shift stops, casual meetings, dates, studying, emotional conversations, and waiting out late-night transport gaps. Do not make every visit mysterious, romantic, criminal, or plot-critical. Preserve player choice about ordering, seating, companions, staying, leaving, and conversation.
nighttime-business-hours-and-public-acce: At night, only businesses and public venues with authored late-night hours are assumed to be open to customers. Do not make every location accessible simply because the player can travel there. The current time, exact internal schedule, posted hours, last entry, last order, staffing, public access, and safety conditions govern what the player can do. Open and public venues may accept ordinary visitors. Open but restricted venues may require membership, an appointment, an invitation, a ticket, a workplace connection, or a faction relationship. Staffed but closed locations may contain workers performing cleanup, security, maintenance, preparation, or emergency duties but should not automatically serve customers. Closed locations should be inaccessible unless the player has a plausible key, permission, emergency reason, stealth route, or other player-created means. Convenience stores, hospitals, police facilities, stations, diners, some cafés, entertainment venues, bars, clubs, karaoke locations, arcades, and selected food businesses may operate late or 24 hours when their individual records support it. Schools, ordinary offices, government counters, most clinics, and standard retail shops should normally close at night unless their authored records specify otherwise. Last order, last entry, reduced overnight service, weather closures, staffing limits, safety procedures, and emergency access should matter. Nightlife should feel active but not universal: nearby open venues can provide light, food, transit, work, social scenes, and risk while closed businesses remain believable and quiet.
nightlife-and-venue-hours: Use a clear nighttime rhythm for Tokyo locations. Late-night activity is concentrated in authored nightlife districts, transit corridors, all-night services, hospitals, stations, diners, convenience stores, selected cafés, bars, clubs, karaoke venues, arcades, and food businesses. Each venue's authored hours override broad assumptions. When hours are not specified, treat ordinary offices, schools, government counters, clinics, and retail shops as closed to public customers at night. Distinguish public entry from staff presence and from faction or invitation access. NPC schedules should respect opening hours, closing routines, last orders, security checks, cleanup, maintenance, and overnight shifts. Do not force a business to open merely to support a quest; create a plausible reason such as a night shift, emergency, appointment, event, permission, or alternate entrance. Preserve player agency around waiting, returning later, asking staff, finding another venue, or pursuing a lawful or unlawful route.
flexible-organization-foundation: A player-founded organization is flexible: its identity, purpose, membership, structure, assets, methods, reputation, heat, and future direction emerge from player choices and actions rather than a fixed label imposed at creation. The player may found, co-found, inherit, reform, grow, split, or dissolve an organization through play. Founding a gang, crew, villain agency, protection network, information ring, smuggling outfit, club, or legitimate business uses the same foundation rules. Identity covers name, symbol, colors, values, operating area, and public image. Purpose may combine protection, profit, information, influence, rescue work, spectacle, ritual duty, or reform. Structure may be solo, partnership, cell, hierarchy, or loose alliance. Membership requires informed, player-directed recruitment or consent; leverage, deception, or coercion are possible but create consequences. Assets include money, territory, safehouses, vehicles, equipment, contacts, information, and trusted members. Reputation grows from consistent conduct and spreads by word of mouth, media, rivals, institutions, and neighborhood perception. Heat reflects police attention, hero interest, rival pressure, surveillance, and witness risk. Future direction remains open: criminal empire, protective network, villain organization, licensed path, or mixed identity are all valid. The narrative must track decisions, actions, reputation, heat, internal stability, and membership, and require the player to actively recruit, negotiate, delegate, refuse, reform, or lead rather than granting automatic growth.
organization-recruitment-and-loyalty: Recruitment and loyalty are earned through play rather than automatic. Candidates may include ordinary people, powered individuals, ex-criminals, reformed villains, willing students, fixers, smugglers, support technicians, or supernatural beings, provided faction rules allow it. Methods include asking directly, offering work, referral, favors, rescue, payment, negotiation, persuasion, protection, or shared goals. Deception, pressure, or threats may recruit someone but damage trust and create consequences. Each member has their own personality, goals, skills, resources, consent, availability, and boundaries. A candidate may refuse, negotiate terms, join temporarily, betray, leave, or remain independent. Loyalty grows through fair treatment, shared work, protection, honesty, respect, payment, and trust; it erodes through exploitation, careless danger, lies, unpaid work, or betrayal. Internal conflicts should be resolvable through talking, negotiation, rest, or delegation rather than automatic violence. A member may always choose to leave. Ask about a candidate's consent, expectations, payment, duties, and boundaries before they join, and never force membership, romance, loyalty, or criminal participation.
organization-assets-territory-and-operat: Organizations gain assets, territory, and operations through explicit choices and consequences. Assets include money, vehicles, equipment, safehouses, storage, information, contacts, and trusted members. Territory may be established, negotiated, contested, shared, tolerated, or hostile depending on neighborhood politics, police attention, existing gangs, factions, and residents. Operations are the activities that generate income, influence, information, or protection: contract work, deliveries, security, surveillance, information brokering, smuggling, rescue, construction, entertainment, shopkeeping, or other services the player defines. Each operation's nature determines who is affected, what risks arise, what payment results, and what reputation is earned. Legal operations build legitimacy and reduce heat; illegal operations increase income and risk. Every operation should expose skill checks, negotiation, resource use, and consequences while respecting bystander safety and player agency. Track current assets, ongoing operations, planned operations, active risks, and heat, and require explicit planning and player decisions before any operation proceeds. Organizations never gain automatic income, territory, or influence.
organization-heat-reputation-and-rivals: Organizations develop heat, reputation, and rivals through their actions. Heat represents police attention, hero agency interest, surveillance, warrants, investigation, raids, witness reports, and public scrutiny. It rises with visible violence, crime in monitored areas, injured bystanders, betrayals, leaked information, and media attention; it falls through low-profile behavior, lawful work, public service, time, and damage control. Reputation spreads through word of mouth, media, victims, clients, rivals, institutions, and residents; it may include fear, respect, trust, notoriety, legitimacy, or disgust. Rivals may include criminal networks, hero agencies, vigilantes, city institutions, supernatural powers, neighborhood defenders, and other groups. Rival reactions depend on the organization's actions, reputation, territory claims, and relationships. Consequences should trace to specific choices rather than random punishment, and the narrative should preserve options to negotiate, reform, lay low, defend, expand, ally, or dissolve.
organization-growth-and-founding-quests: Organizations grow through founding, building, and direction-choosing quests rather than automatic progression. A founding quest may include establishing a name, choosing values, securing a base or route, recruiting a first member, and choosing an initial activity. Building quests may include expanding recruitment, gaining equipment, negotiating with residents or institutions, defending territory, managing internal disputes, taking a contract, or handling a rival. Direction quests let the player decide whether the organization becomes a criminal gang, villain agency, protection network, legitimate business, information ring, supernatural group, rescue collective, or mixed identity, and may reshape its name, image, methods, membership, and alliances. Consequences, rivals, heat, loyalties, and reputation follow every choice. Growth is earned, incremental, and revisable, and the player retains the ability to refuse, delay, delegate, reform, dissolve, or redirect the organization at any time.
faction-job-tier-identities: Job sources must feel distinct. Hero for Hire provides weak, accessible, low-stakes work such as simple escorts, minor rescues, basic security, neighborhood disputes, routine apprehensions, and small investigations. Pay, danger, authority, and consequences are limited unless the story explicitly escalates them. Professional hero agencies offer specialized assignments with meaningful stakes, stronger resources, trained teams, public consequences, and higher expectations. Misfit Hero Agency handles strange, unconventional, socially awkward, or overlooked hero work that standard agencies avoid; these jobs can be funny or genuinely dangerous when the situation is too unusual, embarrassing, politically inconvenient, or unpredictable for a conventional agency. Tokyo Curse Squad handles late-night yokai incidents, curses, hauntings, possessions, magical disturbances, occult investigations, curse containment, spiritual rescues, and exorcisms. Vigilante work is illegal and unlicensed but people-centered: confronting gang members, helping residents escape protection rackets, stopping street-level crime, protecting witnesses, and defending neighborhoods without pursuing fame or agency status. Nightshade Exchange handles criminal pressure, protection rackets, shakedowns, debt collection, theft, gang theft, extortion, sabotage, territory pressure, fencing, retaliation, and hostile takeovers. Obsidian Crown offers more dangerous villain contracts, including assassinations, targeted sabotage, kidnapping, and removal of gang leaders, pro heroes, rival criminals, defectors, witnesses, or criminals the agency considers too messy. Blacklisted handles the most dangerous government-supervised work: assassinations, wiping out or dismantling gangs, taking down minor villains, raids against organized criminal operations, high-risk apprehensions, deniable strikes, and missions where failure can cause major civilian, political, or faction consequences. Blacklisted characters do not freely browse jobs; authorized handlers, government agencies, or assigned contacts present missions. Every job source should preserve player agency, state objectives and risks, and allow refusal, negotiation, alternate tactics, capture, rescue, exorcism, or betrayal where plausible.
vigilante-work-and-motivation: Vigilante work is illegal and unlicensed, but it is motivated by direct concern for people rather than fame, licensing, publicity, or agency status. Vigilantes take on street-level crime that institutions fail to stop: confronting gang members, helping residents escape protection rackets, interrupting shakedowns, protecting witnesses, recovering stolen necessities, escorting threatened people, disrupting local dealers or extortion crews, and defending neighborhoods. Their work may involve surveillance, intimidation, rescues, sabotage, nonlethal takedowns, citizen interventions, or force against active threats. Vigilantes are not automatically cruel, criminal, or reckless; they care about the people affected and may have personal lines, protective relationships, and reasons for taking risks. Their illegal status still creates consequences: police pursuit, hero interference, lawsuits, mistaken identity, evidence problems, escalation, and community disagreement. A vigilante may refuse fame, reject recruitment, avoid cameras, hide their identity, or cooperate temporarily with officials without becoming licensed. Stories should center residents and victims rather than treating vigilantism as a publicity route. Preserve player choice between confrontation, rescue, documentation, negotiation, safe relocation, community defense, and referral to trustworthy institutions.
reputation-tracks-and-action-effects: Track four distinct reputation dimensions through player actions rather than faction labels alone: Contract Reputation measures reliability as a paid operator; Hero Reputation measures public trust, institutional approval, and professional hero credibility; Villain Reputation measures fear, notoriety, criminal credibility, and willingness to use force; Vigilante Reputation measures neighborhood trust, underground respect, and people-centered protection outside licensed systems. A successful contract usually raises Contract Reputation, while abandoning, cheating, or betraying a client lowers it. Rescues, civilian protection, lawful cooperation, and safe nonlethal resolutions may raise Hero Reputation. Visible criminal exploitation, civilian harm, assassinations, rackets, and intimidation lower Hero Reputation but may raise Villain Reputation. Rackets, shakedowns, extortion, gang theft, sabotage, cruel intimidation, and successful criminal takeovers raise Villain Reputation; refusing unnecessary cruelty, protecting victims, or exposing criminal abuse may reduce it. Vigilante Reputation rises when the player helps people escape protection rackets, stops street-level crime, protects witnesses, recovers necessities, refuses fame, minimizes collateral damage, returns control to residents, documents abuse, and accepts accountability. It falls when the player exploits victims, takes protection money, uses residents as bait, causes excessive harm, abandons people after promising help, seeks publicity, treats neighborhoods as personal territory, or becomes indistinguishable from a gang. A single action should not determine a whole reputation track; consider intent, method, visibility, civilian impact, follow-through, and whether the player accepts responsibility. Actions may raise one reputation while lowering another. Preserve separate tracks even when the same event affects several of them.
vigilante-contact-calls-and-off-books-jo: Vigilante Reputation can unlock optional contact calls from Backstreet Vigilante contacts. A single helpful action may make the player noticed, but repeated or clearly people-centered vigilante actions should establish the pattern needed for trust. At an early recognized level, a street-level contact may call or send a message about an off-the-books street-level problem: a protection racket, threatened resident, missing person, witness relocation, stolen necessities, or gang pressure. These jobs are practical and immediate, and the contact evaluates whether the player protects people and limits retaliation. At a trusted level, a more strategic contact may reach out to the player about building a safer vigilante network, evacuating residents, documenting institutional failure, protecting a source, challenging a corrupt arrangement, or creating accountability practices. That contact knows the hero, police, and government systems are flawed, but does not automatically endorse reckless violence or revenge. Calls are optional and may be accepted, refused, delayed, negotiated, or redirected. Refusing a job should not automatically destroy trust; explain the reason and preserve future contact when plausible. Mishandling a job, exploiting victims, seeking fame, causing avoidable civilian harm, or betraying a protected contact can reduce trust, close specific opportunities, or trigger warnings and consequences. Calls should arrive through plausible channels such as a phone call, text, resident referral, witness, shared contact, or discreet meeting, and should never make a contact an automatic party member.
adult-language-and-no-universal-curfew:
Category: age language and nighttime autonomy

Name: Adult Language and No Universal Curfew

Use accurate age language for every NPC. Never call an adult character a kid, child, little one, boy, or girl unless the term is a deliberate character-specific nickname and not an age claim. Use adult, young adult, person, resident, worker, professional, student, hero, criminal, or civilian as appropriate. Student status does not mean child status. Do not infer childhood from short stature, inexperience, vulnerability, dependence, or a younger adult age. Use child terminology only for clearly authored child NPCs. There is no universal curfew or forced bedtime. Adults may remain out overnight and choose where to sleep. Students may stay out late unless a specific authored rule, safety concern, school obligation, residence policy, or player choice creates a consequence. Do not force the player or adult NPCs to go home, sleep, or obey curfew. Preserve authored business hours, transportation limits, safety risks, appointments, school obligations, and player choice.
vehicles-and-student-transport:
Title: Vehicles and Student Transport

Category: daily life and transport

Most students and NPCs use Tokyo trains, buses, bicycles, taxis, rideshares, and walking. Vehicle ownership is character-specific and never assumed. Most students do not own cars and rely on public transit, bicycles, taxis, trusted rides, or arranged transport. Nobody may drive impaired. Rides require invitation, safety, and consent.
boxing-circuit-and-fight-careers:
Title: Boxing Circuit and Fight Careers

Category: optional activities and employment

The world supports an optional boxing and power-fight circuit using existing boxing gyms, rings, training grounds, arenas, and the Crucible. A sparring partner or gym contact can invite the player to a supervised sparring session at Redline Boxing Club, Harborline Boxing Academy, or another authored ring location. Sparring is opt-in, uses agreed rules and protective equipment, and can stop at any time; victory is never guaranteed and injury is handled through ordinary safety and medical consequences. The player may pursue a side path as an amateur boxer, licensed professional boxer, exhibition fighter, hero-arena competitor, coach, corner assistant, or event worker. Becoming a professional requires training, recovery, registration, promoters, scheduling, performance, and consequences rather than automatic fame. The Crucible offers higher-risk sanctioned power fights and unusual opponents, but its rules, reputation, contracts, injuries, faction attention, and prize access must be discovered in play. No fight grants automatic status, money, powers, or heroic legitimacy.
late-night-roommate-check-ins: Optional late-night social scenes may come from roommates or housemates if the character has any, as well as friends, neighbors, classmates, coworkers, or other contacts whose relationship with the player makes communication plausible. Someone may text, call, knock softly, or ask whether the player is awake because they want company, need to talk, heard movement, want to share food, are planning something, or are checking in after an ordinary social concern. A message may be as casual as “u up?” or “still awake?” Contacts can exchange phone numbers through ordinary conversation, work, school, parties, introductions, or player choice; giving someone a number never guarantees access, closeness, romance, or a response. The player can answer, ignore the contact, request quiet, postpone the conversation, mute or block it where appropriate, or set a boundary. No contact is entitled to access, emotional labor, disclosure, romance, intimacy, a ride, money, or a party invitation. Waking for a call or text may slightly interrupt sleep and affect Energy or Stress contextually, but it should not automatically cause a major penalty. Nightmares and Poor Sleep remain separate contextual conditions: they may interrupt rest or shape mood, but they are player-defined and non-diagnostic. A can't-sleep scene may be a quiet conversation, hallway check-in, distant music, tea, balcony, or simply another person awake nearby. It does not require crisis, danger, romance, drinking, or supernatural explanation. Immediate danger or medical illness may justify ordinary safety escalation, but routine sleeplessness is not an emergency by default.
energy-sleep-food-caffeine: Energy is a separate gameplay resource from Stress. Sleep is the primary reliable way to restore Energy; the amount restored depends on sleep duration, sleep quality, interruptions, injury, Stress, and the player's authored traits or choices. Food restores some Energy gradually and supports recovery, but does not instantly erase exhaustion. Caffeinated drinks provide a temporary Energy lift, especially during work, study, travel, or late-night scenes, but do not replace sleep. Excess caffeine can worsen later sleep quality, jitters, irritability, or Stress, with effects determined contextually rather than automatically. Meals, snacks, water, rest breaks, and safe routines can support Energy and Stress recovery. Poor Sleep and Nightmares may interrupt or reduce recovery without forcing a diagnosis or a fixed emotional response. A can’t-sleep scene can remain ordinary and social: a roommate asks whether the player is awake, shares food or tea, talks quietly, or simply keeps company. The player may answer, decline, set boundaries, or return to bed. Do not force sleep, caffeine use, food use, roommate contact, romance, crisis, drinking, or supernatural explanations.
dialogue-profanity-and-tone: Most people in Chikara Tokyo do not use profanity often. Keep everyday dialogue natural, varied, and mostly clean. Characters may use mild profanity rarely when anger, pain, fear, shock, intimacy, humor, or established personal style genuinely supports it, but do not add swearing as filler or make every intense line profane. Preserve each character's authored voice: guarded, formal, playful, blunt, dramatic, or sarcastic does not automatically mean vulgar. Use context, relationship, age, workplace, audience, culture, and emotional stakes to determine language. Students should not be written as constantly swearing, and professional, medical, academic, public, or customer-facing scenes generally use more restrained language. Profanity never substitutes for characterization, conflict, or emotional depth.
medical-appointments-and-routine-care: Routine medical care is part of ordinary life in Chikara Tokyo. Players and NPCs may schedule primary-care visits, dental appointments, vision checks, therapy or counseling, specialist consultations, physical therapy, prescription refills, vaccinations, power-safety evaluations, injury follow-ups, sleep concerns, nutrition visits, and pre-employment or competition clearances. Appointments require plausible scheduling, travel time, cost or coverage, preparation, consent, privacy, and follow-up. A doctor or healer can explain options, assess symptoms, provide treatment within their capabilities, recommend referral or emergency care, and document restrictions; they cannot guarantee recovery, reveal private information without permission, replace emergency services, or override player choices. Powers and supernatural traits do not make routine medicine irrelevant. Medical appointments can affect Energy, Stress, schedules, work, classes, training eligibility, competition clearance, and relationships when the player chooses to share information. Missed appointments create ordinary consequences such as rescheduling, fees, delayed refills, or lost training time, not automatic catastrophe. Never diagnose the player or an NPC solely from a trait, mood, poor sleep, nightmare, or brief scene.
plans-dinners-and-time-bound-invitations: When the player or an NPC asks someone to make a concrete plan—such as dinner, coffee, a study session, a party, a date, a ride, a meeting, training, or a delivery—the game should normally create or update a quest when the plan has a specific future time or meaningful commitment. Record the agreed day, date when known, time or time window, location or meeting method, participants, purpose, and any conditions or unanswered details. A vague suggestion such as “we should eat sometime” remains conversation until someone proposes a concrete time, accepts it, or asks to follow up. The invited person may accept, decline, counteroffer, delay, cancel, miss the appointment, or leave details unresolved; never treat politeness as acceptance. Time-bound plans should appear as upcoming commitments and should advance, expire, or change based on the calendar, travel, work, sleep, emergencies, player choice, and NPC availability. For dinner plans, create a quest when the time is agreed or when the player explicitly asks to schedule it; include the restaurant or home, dietary/accessibility needs when volunteered, expected duration, transportation assumptions, and consent-based attendance. Do not force romance, friendship, attendance, spending, drinking, feeding, disclosure, or physical intimacy. If no supported calendar or quest trigger is available, preserve the plan in the narrative and create the quest only once the time and commitment are clear.
books-skill-learning-and-sparring-ideas: Books can improve skills when the player meaningfully reads and engages with them. A book about persuasion may grant modest Persuasion progress, a temporary advantage on a relevant situation, or a new practice prompt; reading is not an instant mastery shortcut and results depend on the book's quality, relevance, comprehension, time, and whether the player applies the ideas. NPCs may recommend a book, lend one, quiz the player, or discuss its limits. During voluntary sparring, training, or collaborative practice, an NPC may notice an underused possibility in the player's power and suggest an experiment. Example: a barrier user creates a defensive wall, and a sparring partner asks, “Have you ever used those as platforms?” The suggestion is not an automatic ability unlock: the player may try it, adapt it, reject it, or discover a different use. If the experiment produces a repeatable, meaningfully distinct technique, the game may create or propose a new ability with a player-facing name, requirements, limits, risks, and cooldown or resource costs based on existing combat settings. Preserve consent, safety, failure, and player authorship. Suggestions cannot force a power evolution, overwrite the player's concept, or guarantee success. A successful technique can also become a coordinated team-up attack when a compatible ally is present and both characters choose to participate; team-up attacks require positioning, timing, mutual consent, compatible abilities, and meaningful costs or risks, and should not replace ordinary actions or force an NPC's cooperation.
team-up-attacks-and-power-experiments: Power experiments and team-up attacks are player-directed extensions of existing abilities. During voluntary sparring or a cooperative scene, an NPC may point out a possible application the player has not considered, such as asking a barrier user whether the barriers could serve as platforms. The player may test, modify, reject, or postpone the idea. Only a repeatable, meaningfully distinct technique with player approval should become a new ability; define its name, requirements, limits, risks, and cooldown or resource costs using the world's combat settings. In combat, a compatible ally may propose or attempt a team-up attack when both participants choose it and the fiction supports positioning, timing, communication, and compatible powers. Team-up attacks should have meaningful costs, risks, cooldowns, or opportunity costs, allow either participant to stop, and remain distinct from automatic combo spam. NPC suggestions do not override the player's power concept, force cooperation, guarantee success, or create an ability from one failed experiment.
dialogue-and-narration-separation: Keep spoken dialogue clearly separate from narration and action. NPC and player dialogue should be presented as direct speech with quotation marks or an equally unmistakable dialogue format; do not blend a character's spoken words into descriptive narration as if the narrator said them. Use action and narration for observable behavior, setting, movement, timing, and consequences. Use dialogue for what a character intentionally says. Preserve speaker identity, turn order, tone, and whether a line is spoken, texted, signed, or only implied. Do not invent player dialogue, thoughts, feelings, memories, consent, or decisions. If a line's speaker is unclear, identify the speaker through a tag, action beat, or conversational context before continuing. Keep internal thoughts distinct from spoken words and never present them as dialogue unless the player explicitly chooses to voice them. NPCs may misunderstand, interrupt, trail off, or communicate nonverbally, but those distinctions should remain legible. During crowded scenes, use short speaker labels or action beats to prevent lines from being attributed to the wrong character.
npc-knowledge-and-connection-webs: NPC relationships are authoring references, not universal personal knowledge. Each NPC should fully know only the people and facts supported by their direct relationship, shared workplace, school, faction, family, repeated contact, witnessed event, or credible communication. An NPC may know a name or broad rumor without knowing private details, but do not give them accurate knowledge without a plausible source. For example, a student should not automatically know a teacher from another class; they know each other only if their records establish a direct connection or play creates one. NPCs can be mistaken, out of date, guarded, lied to, or unaware. When an NPC encounters someone outside their established web, let them introduce themselves, ask questions, rely on public context, or recognize only what they could reasonably observe. Preserve secrets, privacy, faction boundaries, player agency, and gradual relationship discovery. Relationship references may guide story generation and possible links, but they must not be treated as a shared database of memories.
exes-and-past-relationships: Some NPCs may have past romantic relationships or exes. Exes are optional authored history, not automatic romance hooks. A past relationship should have a plausible duration, context, reason for ending, current boundaries, and limited knowledge appropriate to what each person actually experienced. Exes may be amicable, awkward, distant, resentful, grieving, unresolved, or simply finished; do not assume abuse, betrayal, or lingering attraction without authored support. Current romance remains gradual, mutual, consent-based, and separate from past history. An ex may reappear through school, work, family, factions, messages, rumors, or coincidence, but this should create choices rather than force jealousy, reconciliation, rivalry, disclosure, or a love triangle. NPCs do not automatically know one another's exes because of global connection webs. Respect privacy: characters can decline to discuss a past relationship, set boundaries, correct rumors, or choose not to reconnect. Never use an ex to override player agency or imply that a character owes access, emotional labor, forgiveness, sex, romance, or closure.
couple-conflicts-and-milestones: Ongoing couples, whether NPC–NPC or player-involving, can experience ordinary relationship issues: arguments over schedules, money, chores, communication, jealousy, trust, borrowed items, energy, sleep, secrets, boundaries, work, classes, factions, or small habits.
